life.economy: The Ptolemies worked the island as a royal estate, and the proceeds of its copper, timber and wine went to the treasury at Alexandria. Its forests kept the fleet in hulls, Cyprus being the main base of the Ptolemaic navy outside Egypt for close to two centuries, with the chief yard at Nea Paphos. Mints at Paphos and Salamis struck large quantities of Ptolemaic silver and bronze between about 200 and 80 BCE, the island being better supplied with silver than Egypt itself, and Athens and Alexandria were the steady partners in trade.
life.language: Koine Greek became the language of government, and the Greek alphabet finally displaced the Cypriot syllabary that had carried the island's Greek for some six centuries. The last securely dated syllabic inscriptions come from the rural shrine at Kafizin and belong to about 225 to 218 BCE, though some scholars would keep the script alive later still; the three hundred or so inscribed vessels dedicated there by a man named Onasagoras are mostly alphabetic, with a handful still syllabic or written in both scripts at once. Phoenician, the language of Kition's kings, went out with the dynasty Ptolemy I destroyed in 312 BCE, and the island's last Phoenician inscriptions are third century.
life.religion: Aphrodite's sanctuary at Palaipaphos remained the greatest shrine on the island, its cult image not a statue but a tall conical black stone, and its chief priests were the Cinyradae. The Ptolemies added themselves to the pantheon: about thirty Cypriot inscriptions honour Arsinoe Philadelphus, many of them plain sandstone altars set up privately at Soloi, Chytroi, Idalion, Kourion and Salamis, and a text from Idalion dated 254 BCE names her eponymous priestess. By the late third century the strategos who governed Cyprus was also archiereus, high priest of the whole island, with its sanctuaries and their revenues in his hands.
life.people: Ptolemy I put an end to the city kingdoms: Pumayyaton of Kition was executed in 312 BCE, Stasioikos of Marion was arrested and his city destroyed with its people moved to Nea Paphos, and Nikokreon of Salamis was forced to take his own life in 311 or 310 BCE, the sources differing. Garrisons sat in every town under a single governor who was general and high priest together, residing first at Salamis and later at Nea Paphos, founded about 312 BCE and the first place to serve as capital of the entire island. No usable population figure survives for the period, and any number offered for Hellenistic Cyprus is a guess.

life.economy: Copper was the island's name and its business: Roman aes cyprium, Cyprian metal, gave Latin cuprum and eventually the English word, and the hundred or so ancient slag heaps in the Troodos hold an estimated four million tonnes of waste, the by-product of perhaps 200,000 tonnes of metal smelted over some three thousand years on the geologist George Constantinou's reckoning. Radiocarbon dating puts the great red heap at Skouriotissa at between 73 and 26 BCE, and output there rose to a genuinely industrial scale in late antiquity. In 13 or 12 BCE Augustus gave Herod the Great half the revenue of the Cypriot mines and the management of the other half, a grant known only from Josephus; wine, olive oil, grain, timber, glass and shipbuilding filled out the trade, and provincial coin was struck at Paphos and Salamis.
life.language: Greek was the language of daily life and of nearly all writing, and the whole Roman period has left no more than about eighty Latin inscriptions on the island, a fair measure of how little Latin travelled beyond the governor's offices. The coinage tracks the shift neatly, issues under Augustus and Tiberius being in Latin, Claudian ones bilingual and everything after that in Greek. Paphos and the west kept an imperial calendar devised for Augustus, while Salamis went on using the Egyptian calendar it had inherited from the Ptolemies.
life.religion: Three shrines held the right of asylum and Tacitus names them: Aphrodite at Paphos, Aphrodite at Amathus, and Zeus at Salamis, the first and last of which appear on the island's coins. Emperors were worshipped alongside the old gods rather than in temples of their own, and how much authority the koinon of Cyprus actually exercised over the island's religion is disputed among scholars. Christianity came early, Paul and Barnabas landing at Salamis about 45 CE and converting the proconsul Sergius Paulus at Paphos, though it spread slowly in the countryside; the Jewish revolt of 115 to 117 CE under Artemion wrecked Salamis and ended with the Jews expelled, Cassius Dio's figure of 240,000 dead being rhetoric rather than a count.
life.people: Cyprus became a senatorial province under a proconsul in 22 BCE with Nea Paphos as its capital, garrisoned so lightly that there is no evidence of anything beyond the governor's bodyguard. No reliable population figure exists for the province, though the theatre at Salamis seated some 15,000 and the city's necropolis sprawled across several square kilometres. Earthquakes shaped the age: the shock of 76 CE brought down three cities, which the ancient sources decline to name, and those of about 332 and 342 CE left Salamis and Paphos in ruins, after which Constantius II remitted four years of taxes and rebuilt Salamis on a smaller scale as Constantia.

life.economy: Justinian's law of 536 detached Cyprus from the eastern prefecture and attached it to the quaestura exercitus, so that its grain, olive oil and wine went by sea to provision the Danube army, and the island's economy grew steadily more tied to Constantinople. Copper mining reached its peak here rather than its end: the exposed slag at Skouriotissa formed between about 320 and 520 CE, and Vasiliki Kassianidou has shown extraction surviving the Arab raids and continuing into the eighth century in the north west. Cypriot cooking pots from Dhiorios, made in something like factory conditions, were still reaching Palestine and even the Adriatic in the eighth century, which is the best evidence against the old picture of total collapse.
life.language: Greek replaced Latin in the imperial administration during the seventh century, and Cyprus followed the empire. Modern Cypriot Greek descends not from the ancient Arcadocypriot of the syllabary but from Byzantine medieval Greek, and its divergence is usually put down to the island being cut off from the rest of the Greek world between the seventh and tenth centuries; no vernacular Cypriot text survives from the period, so the early dialect is reconstructed rather than read. Arabic was present through the condominium and through the Maronite communities, some of whom were settled well before 1191, but no word in the dialect can be securely traced to that contact.
life.religion: The Church of Cyprus won its independence from Antioch at the Council of Ephesus in 431, and the Quinisext Council of 692 confirmed it; when Justinian II moved the Cypriots to Nea Justinianoupolis near Cyzicus in 691 the archbishop kept his rank, and after the return in 698 or 699 he kept the title of Nea Justiniana and All Cyprus that his successors bear still. Tradition holds that Archbishop Anthemios found the tomb of Barnabas about 478 and that a grateful Emperor Zeno granted the archbishops the right to sign in red ink, wear imperial purple and carry a sceptre rather than a crosier, though Joseph Huffman has argued that these regalia privileges were in truth a sixteenth century construction. The condominium made the island a refuge during iconoclasm, and the great monasteries followed: Saint John Chrysostomos at Koutsovendis about 1070, Kykkos about 1100 under Alexios I, and Machairas, granted its whole mountain and stavropegial standing by Manuel I in 1172.
life.people: No scholarly population estimate for Byzantine Cyprus can be had, and the figures in circulation should be treated as guesses. Earthquakes struck Salamis in 332 and again ten years later, the second reportedly levelling whatever the sea had not taken, and Jerome found Paphos with nothing but ruins to show what it had been; the plague of Justinian is nowhere actually attested for the island, though Sir George Hill thought it inconceivable that Cyprus escaped. The Arab raids from 649 emptied the coast, Constantia being sacked and its people drifting to Famagusta while Kourion's survivors moved inland to Episkopi, and people came the other way too, with some 3,350 Armenian and Persian prisoners deported to the island under Maurice and Armenian troops settled after the reconquest of 965, although Luca Zavagno argues the destruction has been much overdrawn.

life.economy: Sugar was the kingdom's great industry, grown and refined at Kouklia and Akhelia on the royal estates, at Kolossi under the Knights of Saint John and at Episkopi under the Venetian Cornaro, whose refinery employed four hundred hands in 1494; no sound export tonnage survives, though Pegolotti thought Cypriot sugar the best made anywhere and much of it went to the Martini house in Venice. Salt from the lake at Larnaca was a crown monopoly which every adult on the island was obliged to buy, raising some 80,000 besants a year in the 1390s and shipped on to Syria and Venice, while the camlet cloth woven by the women of Famagusta served as the very currency in which the kingdom paid its tribute, valued in Egypt at twenty ducats the piece. The fall of Acre in 1291 made Famagusta the chief entrepot of the Levant, its customs farmed in 1395 for 37,700 white besants, but the Genoese seizure of the port in 1373 and the Mamluk victory at Khirokitia in 1426, after which Janus was ransomed for 200,000 ducats and the island owed Cairo 5,000 ducats a year, broke the kingdom's finances for good.
life.language: French was the language of the court and of the Haute Cour, and the Assizes of Jerusalem were written in it before being turned into Greek in the fifteenth century and into Italian by 1531; Latin served the church and the charters, Italian rose with the Genoese and Venetians, and Greek remained the tongue of the great majority. The Cypriot Greek dialect became a literary language in its own right, Leontios Machairas writing his Recital concerning the Sweet Land of Cyprus in it in the 1420s and Georgios Boustronios carrying the story on to 1489, while a collection of Petrarchan sonnets in Cypriot Greek, once owned by the humanist Natale Conti and now in the Marciana at Venice, is the only known Petrarchism in the Greek language. Old French had its writers here too, chief among them Philippe de Novare, whose chronicle of the war against Frederick II survives inside the Gestes des Chiprois, and Guillaume de Machaut, who wrote nine thousand verses on Peter I's sack of Alexandria without ever setting foot on the island.
life.religion: A Latin hierarchy was installed in 1196 with an archbishop at Nicosia and suffragans at Paphos, Limassol and Famagusta, and the settlements of 1220 and 1222 cut the Greek bishops to four and banished them to the villages of Solia, Arsinoe, Lefkara and Karpasia, agreements to which the Greeks were not even a party. Alexander IV's Bulla Cypria of 3 July 1260 made the Latin archbishop sole metropolitan and provided that after Germanos died the Greeks should have no archbishop at all, yet it also capped Latin visitation fees and left the Greek courts standing, which is why Chris Schabel has called it the Magna Carta of the Greeks; it governed the island until 1570. Coercion was rare but memorable, thirteen monks of the house of Kantariotissa being tried over the use of leavened bread in 1231, one dying in prison and twelve burned at Nicosia, an episode without parallel in the Latin east; the Maronites numbered perhaps seven or eight thousand in some thirty villages, the Armenians held a quarter of Nicosia still called Armenia, and the Nestorian merchants of Famagusta, the Lakhas brothers among them, built their own church there about 1360.
life.people: Gilles Grivaud, the standard authority, insists that no population count survives from the Lusignan period and that the curve cannot be drawn in absolute numbers; he works from a deliberately low figure of about 70,000 peasants for the royal accounts of 1412 and 1413, and rejects the 300,000 that circulates without evidence. Nine epidemics between 1347 and 1471 covered eighteen years in all, the Black Death of 1347 and 1348 costing between a third and two thirds of the people according to which chronicler one follows, though J. C. Russell's estimate of about twenty per cent is the sober corrective, and locusts stripped the crops for three or four years after 1409 until Janus ordered the eggs dug out and buried in 1413. Below a Frankish nobility that amounted to only a thousand or twelve hundred people in the thirteenth century sat the paroikoi, who owed two or three days' labour a week and a third of their crops and could be sold or flogged at their lord's will, then the perperiarii and the freed francomati; after Khirokitia the countryside rose in 1426 and a peasant styling himself King Alexis held Lefkoniko until he was hanged on 12 May 1427.

life.economy: Cotton became the boom crop, known as the plant of gold, and by about 1600 it had driven out sugar, whose Cypriot plantations were already failing against Madeira, a competitor the Venetian diarist Marino Sanudo named as early as 1496. Salt from Larnaca was a state monopoly so strict that Venetian ships calling at the island had to dump their ballast and load salt for Venice, and John Locke reported in 1553 that a Venetian caught carrying an ounce out of the city lost an ear; estimates of what the Signory made from it range from 100,000 to 800,000 ducats a year, and Hill thought 300,000 near the truth. Grain was the largest crop of all, its export licensed only after eighteen months' supply had been set aside, and the Proveditor Bernardo Sagredo reckoned the island's whole revenue in 1585 at 546,000 ducats, of which 300,000 came from salt, leaving 361,669 net of the garrison's pay; fortification swallowed much of the rest, 178,092 ducats going on Famagusta between 1491 and 1528 and the Martinengo bastion alone costing 50,000.
life.language: Italian, and specifically the Venetian dialect, became the written language of government, and by 1531 the Assizes had been rendered into it; a French visitor named Mesenge complained in 1507 that pleadings once made in French were now made in Italian, and that Cypriot gentlemen, as good Frenchmen as any in France, were wonderfully ill content to be subjects of Venice. Greek remained the language of the countryside and of the church. The chronicles of the transition make the point neatly, Georgios Boustronios writing his account of 1456 to 1489 in Cypriot Greek prose while his relative Florio Bustron, an administrator under Venice, wrote his Historia overo commentarii de Cipro in Italian, and the 156 Petrarchan poems in Cypriot Greek preserved in the Marciana were probably assembled between 1546 and 1570.
life.religion: The Latin church stayed on top and the Greek church stayed subordinate, with four bishops each answering to the Latin diocesan above him and the Greek archbishopric still vacant under the terms of the Bulla Cypria. Nicholas Coureas argues that in practice the Greek church grew stronger rather than weaker, because the Latins were few and town bound, Rome was distant and the Ottoman threat made enforcement of papal directives unwise; the four Greek bishops drew 1,400 ducats between them about 1500, while eighteen Greek monasteries were reported in 1529 with 6,600. The Maronites lost people back to the Levant under heavy taxation, and the Armenians dwindled too, though they had held their Nicosia quarter and the church of Notre Dame de Tyre since before 1504 and kept shops in Famagusta, Limassol, Paphos and the capital.
life.people: Venetian reports put the island's population somewhere between 100,000 and 200,000 and disagree wildly among themselves: 106,000 from the Cypriot deputation of 1490, 90,000 from the Syndic of 1504 against his Lieutenant's 130,000, 121,179 in the census of 1523, 126,179 from Minio in 1529, 197,000 from Attar about 1540 and 200,000 from Graziani about 1570, on which evidence Hill concluded the population probably rose rather than fell. Serfdom was the ordinary condition: Martin von Baumgarten wrote in 1508 that all the inhabitants were slaves to the Venetians, paying a third of everything and working two days a week for the state, and Hill computes the paroikoi's burden at about forty per cent of produce, a third plus the tithe; every villein, male or married female over fifteen, also paid a besant a head for salt, and in 1490 the Cypriots said many had fled the island rather than bear it. Nicosia held perhaps 21,000 people before the siege of 1570 and roughly that number died in it, the Ottoman survey of 1572 finding between 1,100 and 1,200 left; Famagusta held out from September 1570 to 5 August 1571, and contemporaries put the total Venetian and Cypriot loss at 56,000 killed or enslaved.

life.economy: The Porte farmed the island out, first through timars granted to Lala Mustafa's soldiers and later through annual iltizam and lifetime malikane leases, and the cizye or poll tax on non-Muslims was set in 1572 at eleven, five and a half or three piastres according to means. The imperial rescript of 1754 fixed the island's liability at 10,066 warrants of assessment at twenty-one and a half piastres each, some 216,400 piastres a year, and required that number to be issued whether the population rose or fell; by the 1760s barely 7,500 people were left to pay it, which explains eighteenth century Cyprus better than anything else does. Cotton was the chief export, about 3,000 quintals or 750 tons a year around 1750 going to Britain, France, Holland and Venice, with the French houses at Larnaca acting as factors for merchants of Marseille; Mahmud II fixed the annual tribute at 3,179,082 piastres in 1837, and a British consular return of the 1870s puts total regular revenue at 16,836,874 piastres, of which the salt monopoly alone yielded 2,929,550.
life.language: Ottoman Turkish was the language of administration and of the kadi courts, which non-Muslims and foreigners could also use, while Greek remained the language of the great majority and of the church that collected their taxes. Cypriot Turkish grew out of Ottoman Turkish and the Yoruk dialect of the Taurus, brought by settlers moved from the Karaman region under the settlement law of 22 September 1572, and Sir Harry Luke thought the community had preserved the purity of its Turkish to a degree matched almost nowhere else; the British census of 1881 found 95 per cent of the island's Muslims giving Turkish as their mother tongue, the Greek-speaking remainder falling below two per cent by the 1920s. No literacy rate for Ottoman Cyprus appears to survive, but Archbishop Kyprianos founded the Hellenic School of Nicosia in 1812, the island's first secondary school and now the Pancyprian Gymnasium.
life.religion: The Latin church was suppressed after 1571 and the Orthodox archbishopric restored, Timotheos taking office in 1572 as the first Greek archbishop since 1260, while Saint Sophia in Nicosia and Saint Nicholas in Famagusta became mosques, taking the names Selimiye and Lala Mustafa Pasha only in 1954. Under the millet system the archbishop and his three suffragans rose from spokesmen for their flock, a role the chronicler Kyprianos dates to about 1660, to being the tax intermediaries of the settlement of 1754, so that one British traveller reported that Cyprus was in fact governed by the Greek archbishop and his clergy; that ascendancy ended on 9 July 1821, when the governor Kucuk Mehmet had Archbishop Kyprianos and the three bishops killed along with some 470 to 486 leading Greeks, the count varying by source. Latins, Venetians, Maronites and Armenians converted to Islam to escape the taxes and disabilities laid on non-Muslims and became the Linobambaki, the linen and cotton people who kept a Christian and a Muslim name apiece across seventeen to twenty villages depending on which list one follows, while at Larnaca the Hala Sultan Tekke grew around the tomb of Umm Haram, a shrine built in 1760 with its mosque completed in 1817.
life.people: The conquest emptied the island: 76 villages of the Mesaoria and Mazato were recorded with no inhabitants at all in 1572, Nicosia fell from perhaps 21,000 people to between 1,100 and 1,200, and famine followed the war. The enumerations counted taxpayers rather than people and must be read as such, an examiner about 1641 finding hardly 25,000 rayahs after the dearth of 1640 and the plague of 1641, Archimandrite Kyprianos publishing the census of 1777 as 10,487 Christian tax-paying families in 564 villages, giving 37,000 Christians and 47,000 Muslims while warning that the estimate was approximate and that doubts about the Muslim figure were grave, and the Ottoman register of 1831, which counted males only, returning 14,983 Muslim and 29,190 non-Muslim males, 44,216 in all. Plague took perhaps a third of the island in 1692 and again in 1760, drought and locusts brought a famine in 1757 and 1758 that sent a great number fleeing to Syria and Anatolia, and the tax revolt of 1764 ended with the muhassil Cil Osman and eighteen of his followers killed in the burning palace; the first British census, taken in 1881 three years after the handover, found 186,173 people, 137,631 of them Greek Orthodox and 45,458 Muslim.

life.economy: Under the Cyprus Convention Britain undertook to pay the Ottoman treasury an annual fixed sum of 92,799 pounds, eleven shillings and threepence, more than half the island's average revenue, but the money never reached Istanbul: it was deposited at the Bank of England to service the Ottoman Crimean War loan of 1855 on which the Porte had defaulted, and it was Cypriots who paid both the tribute and the cost of their own administration. Churchill, visiting as Undersecretary in 1907, wrote that Britain had no right except by force majeure to take a penny of the Cyprus Tribute to relieve itself of its own obligations, and Parliament soon voted a permanent grant-in-aid of 50,000 pounds which reduced it accordingly. Copper came back with the Cyprus Mines Corporation, founded in 1916 after Charles Gunther noticed the Roman slag at Skouriotissa, and by 1955 its mines were the island's largest industry and furnished more than a quarter of all government revenue; asbestos was worked at Amiantos in the Troodos until 1988, the Cyprus Government Railway carried 3,199,934 tons of freight between 1905 and 1951 without ever making a profit, and by the 1960s Britain was drinking 13.6 million litres of Cypriot wine a year, half the island's production and most of it sold as sweet sherry.
life.language: English was the official language of the colony and continued in legal proceedings until 1989 and in the legislature until 1963, though Greek and Turkish remained in everyday and communal use. Schooling was divided between Greek and Turkish curricula, and British attempts to curtail Greek influence in the schools were among the stated causes of the revolt of 1931. No literacy rate from the colonial censuses could be traced for this entry, but the growth of Greek secondary education is plain enough in the expansion of the Nicosia Hellenic School into a lyceum in 1893 and the founding of a teacher training college the following year.
life.religion: The Church of Cyprus kept its standing and its politics, and the archbishop remained the ethnarch: Makarios III was elected on 18 September 1950 and the church at once organised the enosis plebiscite of that January, signed in open books placed in the churches, which returned 95.7 per cent in favour, a result taken by some as coerced. Muslim religious property was administered through the Evkaf, over which the 1878 Convention gave Britain a measure of control, with an Ottoman and a British delegate on a board that also seated the mufti and the kadi of Cyprus; Britain gave up that control only in 1956. The church then led the political struggle, Makarios becoming the political head of the EOKA campaign from 1955 and being exiled to the Seychelles in 1956.
life.people: The censuses run every ten years from 1881, with none taken in 1941, and show steady growth: 186,173 in 1881, 237,022 in 1901, 347,959 in 1931, 450,114 in 1946 and 573,566 in 1960, the Greek Orthodox share rising from 73.9 per cent to about 80 by 1946 before settling at 77.1 in 1960, and the Muslim or Turkish share falling from 24.4 per cent to 18.2. Emigration ran outward throughout, with some 30,000 Turkish Cypriots leaving for Turkey between 1881 and 1927 and a Turkish Cypriot community of about 8,500 established in Britain by 1958. The October 1931 riots left seven protesters dead and 2,606 people punished, nine camps at Caraolos, Dhekelia and Xylotymbou held 53,510 Jewish detainees between August 1946 and January 1949, and the malaria campaign begun in 1946 by the Turkish Cypriot health inspector Mehmet Aziz divided the island into 556 blocks and made Cyprus the first malaria-free country in the world by February 1950.

life.economy: The events of 1974 cost the Republic about seventy per cent of its wealth-producing resources, tourist facilities falling by 65 per cent and industry by 46, after which growth averaged 6.1 per cent a year through the 1980s. Services now account for close to eighty per cent of the economy and agriculture for about two, and travel and tourism generate roughly a fifth of GDP, arrivals passing four million for the first time in 2024 and earning about 3.2 billion euros, with the United Kingdom, Israel and Poland the largest markets; the shipping registry is the third largest in the European Union. The euro replaced the Cypriot pound on 1 January 2008 at 0.585274 to one, and the banking crisis of March 2013 brought a ten billion euro programme, the closure of Laiki and the conversion of 47.5 per cent of uninsured deposits at the Bank of Cyprus into shares, some 3.8 billion euros in all; halloumi was registered as a protected designation of origin in 2021 under all three of its names, and the Aphrodite gas field, announced in December 2011, is not expected to produce before 2027.
life.language: Article 3 of the 1960 constitution makes Greek and Turkish the official languages, requires legislative and administrative acts to be drawn up in both, and allows anyone to address the authorities in either. In practice Standard Modern Greek is the high variety and Cypriot Greek, which is unintelligible to an unprepared speaker of the standard, is the language people actually use, and Cypriot Turkish stands in much the same relation to standard Turkish in the north, where the standard became the language of schools and media. English remains widely spoken, by about 73 per cent of the population according to Eurobarometer, and it served in the courts until 1989; Armenian was recognised under the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages on 1 December 2002 and Cypriot Maronite Arabic in 2008, though at the 2011 census none of the 3,656 Maronite Cypriots in the government-controlled area declared it as a first language.
life.religion: Makarios III held the archbishopric and the presidency at once from 1960 until his death in 1977, and when three bishops demanded that he resign the presidency in 1972 he had them defrocked the following summer and enlarged the synod to dilute them. The constitution gives special standing to five bodies, the Church of Cyprus, the Vakif, the Maronites, the Armenian Orthodox and the Latins, and provides that citizens belonging to neither main community must opt to join one of them: the Armenians, recognised as a religious group under Article 2, chose the Greek Cypriot community in a referendum on 13 November 1960. The 2011 census gave the government-controlled area as 89.1 per cent Greek Orthodox among all residents, or 97.4 per cent among Cypriot citizens alone, and the 2021 figure of 74.5 per cent looks like a collapse but chiefly reflects a rise in those declining to state a religion, from 1.1 to 17.3 per cent; the Technical Committee on Cultural Heritage has meanwhile restored or protected more than a hundred churches and mosques on both sides of the line.
life.people: The 1960 census found 573,566 people, 77.1 per cent Greek and 18.2 per cent Turkish, and in the fighting of 1963 and 1964 nearly 25,000 Turkish Cypriots, about a sixth of their community, left their homes for enclaves, Pierre Oberling's figures giving 364 Turkish Cypriot and 174 Greek Cypriot dead. In 1974 between 140,000 and 200,000 Greek Cypriots were displaced from the north, the spread reflecting the difference between people counted crossing and the refugee caseload the government supported, and 50,000 to 60,000 Turkish Cypriots moved north from the south, largely under the Vienna III agreement of August 1975; the Committee on Missing Persons lists 2,002 people missing from 1963 to 1974, 1,510 Greek Cypriots and 492 Turkish Cypriots, of whom 1,081 had been identified by July 2026. The 2021 census counted 923,381 residents in the government-controlled area, 77.9 per cent of them Cypriot citizens, with Greeks, Romanians, Britons, Bulgarians, Syrians and Russians the largest foreign groups, so that about a fifth of the population holds another nationality; the north's last agreed census, in 2011, gave 286,257, and the number of settlers from Turkey remains genuinely contested, the researcher Mete Hatay calling the higher claims wildly speculative.

notes_for_owner: Roman copper: the widely quoted figure is 200,000 tonnes of metal from about four million tonnes of slag across the whole Troodos over roughly 3,000 years (Constantinou, via the Cyprus Tourism Organisation copper itinerary), not 250,000 tonnes and not Roman-only. Wikipedia's Roman Cyprus article says Roman mining was scaled down, which the 2021 Antiquity fieldwork contradicts for late antiquity; the entry follows the fieldwork.

Roman salt: no attestation could be found for Roman-period salt production at the Larnaka or Limassol salt lakes, so it is omitted. The salt industry is only securely documented from the Frankish period onward (Hill).

Population figures for Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine and Lusignan Cyprus: none of the four eras yields a defensible number. The often-quoted 100,000 to 200,000 range is Hill's, and it is for the VENETIAN period only; it should not be carried back into the Lusignan era. Grivaud explicitly rejects the 300,000 that circulates for the Lusignan kingdom.
The Justinianic plague and the Antonine plague of 164 CE are both unattested for Cyprus in the sources; Hill only infers the former. Both are therefore left out.

The Arab tribute of 649 is given in the sources as 7,200 gold pieces or dinars, not nomismata, and al-Baladhuri and al-Tabari give 7,000. Evangelos Chrysos regards the ninth-century Arabic tradition about seventh-century Cyprus as unreliable in principle.
The 965 reconquest was led by Niketas Chalkoutzes, not by Nikephoros Phokas in person, and may have begun as early as mid-964.

Barnabas's tomb: the discovery is dated 478 by Hill and about 488 by Wikipedia; Joseph Huffman (Church History, 2015) argues the archbishop's regalia privileges are a sixteenth-century construction rather than a grant of Zeno. The entry flags the dispute but keeps the traditional date.

Lusignan crown revenue: no canonical annual figure exists. The royal accounts do not survive and Hill says so; the '3,000 florins' sometimes quoted is Ludolf of Sudheim on individual nobles, not the crown.

The Mamluk tribute after 1426 is 5,000 ducats a year with a 200,000 ducat ransom (Hill, who states these are the correct figures). Pero Tafur and Sanudo give 8,000, and Sanudo elsewhere gives 10,000 for ten years; the entry uses Hill's figures.

The Genoese indemnity of 1373: the chroniclers' 900,000 ducats does not appear in the treaty text, which specifies a perpetual tribute of 40,000 gold florins, a fine of 2,012,400 florins over twelve years and 90,000 florins for fleet upkeep. The entry avoids the figure entirely for want of room.

Sugar and cotton export tonnages: no sound figure exists for either the Lusignan or the Venetian period. The '33 tonnes in 1532' figure circulating online is unsourced and the Toronto World Sugar History Newsletter survey gives no production figures at all. The '400 hands' figure is specific to the Cornaro refinery at Episkopi in 1494 and should not be multiplied across the three sites.
Kolossi and Episkopi ownership: Hill and von Wartburg put the Hospitallers at Kolossi and the Cornaro at Episkopi. A 2023 Cyprus Mail feature reverses them; the entry follows Hill.

The Grand Commandery's payments to Rhodes: 12,000 ducats was the usual responsion per Hill, while the Department of Antiquities narrative gives 4,000 from 1468 and an income of 8,000 ducats from 41 villages in 1489. These are different payments and should not be merged.

Venetian plague and famine years: 1533, 1547 and 1542 could not be verified in Hill, Excerpta Cypria or any other source consulted, so they are omitted. Locust damage in 1510 is documented in the fiscal record.

The 1572 surgun: the household figure often given as 1,689 could not be verified anywhere. What is verified is the general settlement law of 22 September 1572 moving families from the Karaman region, and Fra Angelo Calepio's report of about 20,000 disbanded Ottoman troops remaining as settlers, which is a different thing.

The 1831 Ottoman register is frequently misreported. Karpat's table gives 14,983 Muslim and 29,190 non-Muslim MALES, 44,216 in all, males only. The '44,000 Muslim and 100,000 non-Muslim' figures belong to a later series (about 1872) and count whole populations.
An 1825 Ottoman census of Cyprus could not be traced in any source. Plague in 1835 and 1837 could not be verified either and is omitted; 1641, 1692 and 1760 are attested through Kyprianos.

The 1821 killings: 9 July 1821 under Kucuk Mehmet is well attested, with the archbishop and three bishops and 470 to 486 notables. A rival account on the Ottoman Cyprus page gives 15 October 1821 and 'five bishops', which is impossible since Cyprus had four prelates; it should be disregarded.

Carob: the popular epithet 'black gold' could not be verified in any source, so it is not used. Carob is documented as a Cypriot export under the Venetians and in mid-nineteenth-century British consular returns, but no tonnage was found.

Amiantos asbestos: the 1988 closure is verified through the Spitali cableway. The 1904 opening date, the claim that it was Europe's largest asbestos mine, and all output figures could NOT be verified and are omitted.

The Cyprus Tribute's abolition: the 1907 reduction via the 50,000 pound grant-in-aid is verified, but a 1927 abolition or final settlement could not be confirmed. The entry therefore stops at the grant-in-aid. Diana Markides's Cyprus Review article is the source to chase for the 1920s settlement.
The Cyprus Mines Corporation's 'nearly a million tons of copper a year' by 1955 is almost certainly ore rather than metal; the entry uses the revenue share instead, which is soundly documented.

Colonial-era literacy rates and town populations could not be found. The 1881 census report was not locatable online and HathiTrust full-text search was inaccessible. Also unverified: the date English formally became the language of the courts (1935 is often given), the colonial Education Laws, newspaper founding dates, and the abolition of the mufti's office (1928 is often given).

Tourism's share of GDP: about 20 per cent per the US Department of Commerce country commercial guide, with services near 80 per cent of GDP. Wikipedia's Tourism in Cyprus gives only a 2006 figure of 10.7 per cent, which is out of date.

The 1974 displacement figures are irreducibly contested. 150,000, 160,000 and 200,000 all appear in reputable sources for Greek Cypriots, and 50,000, 51,000 and 60,000 for Turkish Cypriots; the differences are definitional (people counted crossing versus assisted refugee caseload versus UN-facilitated transfers). The entry gives ranges and says why.

Settlers from Turkey in the north: no internationally accepted count exists. The 2011 census under UN observation gave 294,906 de jure or 286,257 de facto, and Mete Hatay describes the higher circulating claims as wildly speculative. A 2022 census total could not be found; the figures of 382,836 and 476,214 that circulate are estimates or projections, not censuses.

The 2011 religion figures for Cyprus depend entirely on the denominator: 89.1 per cent Orthodox among all residents, 97.4 per cent among Cypriot citizens alone. Both are 'the 2011 census'. The 2021 fall to 74.5 per cent is largely a non-response artefact, with 17.3 per cent not stating a religion against 1.1 per cent in 2011.

All CYSTAT census figures rest on secondary transcription: cystat.gov.cy is a JavaScript application that no automated fetcher could read, and gov.cy returned 403. The 2021 preliminary results PDF at census2021.cystat.gov.cy does load and is cited. The final total 923,381 should be re-checked against CYSTAT in a browser before publication.

World Bank per-capita GDP figures for Cyprus should not be mixed with IMF ones: the World Bank population series appears to cover the whole island while its GDP series covers only the government-controlled area. The entry avoids per-capita figures for this reason.

Halloumi's exact PDO registration date (commonly 12 April 2021), the milk ratio rule and the Green Line arrangements could not be verified; only the year 2021 and the three registered names are confirmed. The Cronos and Zeus gas discoveries could not be verified at all and are omitted.

The Technical Committee on Cultural Heritage's founding date is given as 2008 on one source and 2012 on the committee's own site (probably the committee versus the UNDP restoration programme). The 'more than 100 sites' figure is the committee's own. No individual monument is named in the entry because the committee's site names none.

The Cypriot Canzoniere's manuscript is Venice, Biblioteca Nazionale Marciana, cod. Gr. cl. IX, 32, with 156 poems (some counts give up to 164). Whether it is one poet's canzoniere or an anthology is contested. The claim sometimes made that it is the first Petrarchan poetry outside Italy is not supported; 'the only known Petrarchism in Greek' is the defensible version and is what the entry says.
